For doctors: practice and guidelines
Can I drink coffee during pregnancy?

Yes, in moderation. Up to 200 mg of caffeine a day (about 1–2 cups of coffee) is not linked to a higher risk of miscarriage or preterm birth. Remember that caffeine is also found in tea, cola, energy drinks and chocolate. It is best to avoid energy drinks altogether.
How much weight is it normal to gain during pregnancy?

It depends on your weight before pregnancy (BMI):
• BMI < 18.5 — 12.5–18 kg
• 18.5–24.9 — 11.5–16 kg
• 25–29.9 — 7–11.5 kg
• ≥ 30 — 5–9 kg
What matters more than the number on the scales is good nutrition and movement. There is no need to "eat for two": almost no extra calories are needed in the 1st trimester, and about +300–450 kcal a day in the 2nd–3rd.
US Institute of Medicine, 2009; WHO
Can I exercise during pregnancy?

Yes, and it is good for you. At least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week is recommended (walking, swimming, pregnancy yoga, exercise bike) if there are no medical contraindications. Avoid sports with a risk of falling or a blow to the abdomen, and lying on your back for long periods after 20 weeks. Regular movement lowers the risk of gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia and excessive weight gain.
WHO, 2020; ACOG
Which vaccines are recommended during pregnancy?

• Flu — during the season, at any stage of pregnancy.
• Whooping cough (Tdap) — at 27–36 weeks in every pregnancy: antibodies pass to the baby and protect it in the first months.
• RSV — at 32–36 weeks (where the vaccine is available), or the baby receives antibodies after birth.
• COVID-19 — according to current recommendations.
Live vaccines (measles, rubella, chickenpox) are not given during pregnancy — they are given before or after.
ACOG; CDC; WHO
How should I keep track of my baby's movements?

There is no "right" number of movements, such as "10 a day". What matters is knowing your own baby's usual pattern. If movements become weaker or less frequent, or their pattern changes, contact the maternity hospital the same day — don't wait until morning or your next appointment. Movements do not decrease before labour.
When should I see a doctor urgently?

Call 103 (ambulance in Ukraine) or go to the maternity hospital immediately if you have: vaginal bleeding; leaking or a gush of fluid; severe abdominal pain; reduced baby movements; severe headache, flashing lights in front of the eyes, sudden swelling of the face and hands; a temperature of ≥ 38 °C; seizures; regular contractions before 37 weeks.
WHO; RCOG
When should I go to the maternity hospital?

• Regular contractions — every 5 minutes for an hour (for a first birth; for later births go earlier, as labour is quicker).\n• Your waters have broken — even without contractions. Note the colour: green or brown fluid means go immediately.\n• Any bleeding, reduced baby movements or severe constant pain — straight away.
Is epidural anaesthesia safe?

Yes, it is the most effective method of pain relief in labour. According to large reviews, it does not increase the caesarean section rate and does not harm the baby. Possible effects: lower blood pressure, itching, raised temperature, a somewhat longer second stage and more frequent use of vacuum extraction. The decision is always yours — we can discuss it in advance.
Can I have a vaginal birth after a caesarean section?

In most cases — yes. After one caesarean section with a transverse uterine incision, vaginal birth succeeds in about 60–80% of women. The risk of uterine rupture is about 0.5–1%, so the birth should take place in hospital where an emergency operation is possible. It is worth discussing your birth plan with your doctor at 34–36 weeks.
How long should I breastfeed?

WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months and continuing alongside solid foods until 2 years and beyond — for as long as mother and baby wish. If breastfeeding doesn't work out, it is not a failure: help from a lactation consultant often solves the problem, and formula is a safe alternative.
WHO / UNICEF
Is it normal to feel sad and tearful after birth?

In the first 2 weeks, many women have the "baby blues": mood swings, tearfulness, anxiety. It passes on its own. If it lasts more than 2 weeks, gets in the way of caring for the baby, or you feel hopeless or have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, it may be postnatal depression. It is very treatable — see a doctor without delay.
ACOG; WHO
When can I get pregnant again?

WHO recommends an interval of at least 24 months from birth to the next conception; an interval of less than 18 months is linked to a higher risk of preterm birth. After a caesarean section — no sooner than 12–18 months. It is worth thinking about contraception in the first weeks — ovulation can return before your first period.
WHO; ACOG
When should I start folic acid, and how much?

0.4–0.8 mg (400–800 mcg) daily from at least 1 month before conception and during the first 2–3 months of pregnancy. This substantially reduces the risk of neural tube defects. Higher doses (4–5 mg) only when prescribed by a doctor for high risk (e.g. a defect in a previous pregnancy, certain medicines).
USPSTF, 2023 (grade A)
How often should I be screened for cervical cancer?

The best method is an HPV (human papillomavirus) test: every 5 years, starting at 25–30 depending on the guideline. The alternative is cytology (Pap smear) every 3 years. HPV vaccination protects against most cases of cervical cancer — it is best given before becoming sexually active, but is useful later too.
WHO, 2021; USPSTF
What is PMOS (formerly PCOS)?

Since May 2026, polycystic ovary syndrome has a new international name — polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). There are no true cysts in the ovaries, and the syndrome affects hormones and metabolism throughout the body. Signs: irregular cycles, acne, excess hair growth, difficulty conceiving. Treatment is based on a healthy lifestyle; effective medicines are available. It is worth checking blood sugar, lipids, blood pressure and mood.
What are the new diagnostic criteria for postpartum haemorrhage?

The 2025 WHO/FIGO/ICM consolidated guidelines propose diagnosing PPH at an objectively measured blood loss of ≥ 500 ml, or ≥ 300 ml with abnormal haemodynamic signs — and immediately starting the MOTIVE bundle (uterine massage, uterotonics, tranexamic acid, IV fluids, examination of the genital tract, escalation) rather than acting step by step. The key is measuring blood loss with calibrated drapes.
Tranexamic acid for PPH: dose and timing?

1 g IV slowly (over 10 min) as early as possible — within 3 hours of birth, regardless of the cause of bleeding. If bleeding continues after 30 min or recurs within 24 h — a second dose of 1 g. Giving it later than 3 hours is not recommended (no benefit).
WHO, 2017/2025; WOMAN trial
Aspirin for pre-eclampsia prevention — who and at what dose?

Women at high risk (or with ≥ 2 moderate risk factors) — low-dose aspirin every evening from 12–16 weeks (ideally before 16) until 36 weeks. FIGO and ISSHP recommend 150 mg (ASPRE), ACOG/USPSTF — 81 mg. Combined first-trimester screening (FMF) identifies the at-risk group more accurately than history alone.
Antenatal corticosteroids: gestational age limits?

Recommended when birth is likely within 7 days at 24⁺⁰–33⁺⁶ weeks (WHO — up to 34⁺⁰), provided gestational age is accurately assessed, there is no infection and appropriate preterm newborn care is available. Course: betamethasone 12 mg IM twice, 24 h apart, or dexamethasone 6 mg IM 4 times, 12 h apart. Routine use in the late preterm period is debated.
WHO, 2022; ACOG
Magnesium sulphate for fetal neuroprotection — when?

When preterm birth is expected before 32 weeks (some guidelines — up to 30⁺⁶), to reduce the risk of cerebral palsy. Typical regimen: 4 g IV loading dose, then 1 g/h until birth or for up to 24 h. Monitor reflexes, breathing and urine output.
WHO, 2022; ACOG CO 455; NICE NG25
Induction of labour at 39 weeks in low-risk women?

According to ARRIVE and subsequent meta-analyses, elective induction at 39⁰–39⁶ weeks in low-risk nulliparous women does not increase — and may reduce — the rates of caesarean section and hypertensive complications. It is an option to discuss with the patient, not a mandatory approach; it requires labour ward resources.
Delayed cord clamping — the standard?

Yes. In term and preterm newborns who do not need immediate resuscitation, the cord is clamped no sooner than 30–60 seconds (WHO — at least 1 min). This improves iron stores and, in preterm babies, reduces mortality and the need for transfusions.
WHO; ACOG CO 814; Cochrane
Group B strep screening — when?

Culture (vagina + rectum) at 36⁰–37⁶ weeks; the result is valid for 5 weeks. Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (penicillin or ampicillin) — with a positive result, GBS bacteriuria during pregnancy, or a previous baby with GBS infection.
